title: Six Spare MacBook Airs Ran a Private LLM Before Lunch
author: piotrgrudzien

excerpt: Six Macs with nothing to do Until recently, six MacBook Airs were our team’s remote development machines. Each one ran a Linux virtual machine full of Docker containers, and we worked inside those containers from our own laptops. Then we moved all of that to Boxes42, the remote development product we build ourselves, and the six Macs had nothing left to do. They ended up on a desk next to mine. Each has an M2 chip and 16 GB of memory. 96 GB and an idea Sixteen gigabytes is not much for a language model, but six of these Macs have 96 GB between them, which is enough for a fairly large one if they can share it. EXO is an open-source tool that splits one model across several Macs, so that each one holds a part of the model and they answer together. I had never tried it, and I wanted to see how it is done. For that the Macs have to be connected, and the fast way to connect Macs is Thunderbolt. A MacBook Air has two Thunderbolt ports, so six of them can be joined in a line, each Mac cabled to the next. That takes five cables. Looking for cables The cables took most of the time. Our office has a drawer full of USB-C cables, and most of them are for charging. They fit the same ports and look much the same as Thunderbolt cables, but they carry little or no data. I found one that worked and connected the first two Macs with it. I decided to get those two running before I went looking for the other four. Handing the setup to Claude I opened Claude Code, which could reach the Macs over SSH, and handed it the setup. It started by shutting down what the Macs still ran from their days as dev machines, which freed most of their memory, and then installed EXO on both. The two Macs then ignored each other. Each one decided it was a cluster of one, and nothing said why. Claude went through EXO’s documentation and found the cause in macOS.
